passages.original: 4): c Dum essem juvenis, et solitudinis me deserta vallarent, incentiva vitiorum, ardoremque naturae ferre non poteram: quem cum crebris jejuniis frangerem, mens tamen cogitationibus aestuabat; ad quam edomandam. cuidam fratri, qui ex Hebraeis crediderat, me in disciplinam dedi, ut post Quintiliani acumina, Ciceronis fluvios, gravitatemque Frontonis, et lenitatem Plinii, alphabetum discerem, et stridentia anhelantiaque 7 verba meditarer. Quid ibi laboris insumpserim, quid sustinuerim difficultatis, quoties desperaverim, quoties cessaverim, et contentione discendi rursus inceperim, testis est conscientia, tam mea qui passus sum, quam eorum qui mecum duxerunt vitam.
passages.english: "When I was a young man, and the wastes of the wilderness walled me in, I could not bear the incitements of the vices and the heat of nature. Though I tried to break it with frequent fasts, my mind still seethed with thoughts. To tame it, I gave myself as a pupil to a certain brother who had come to the faith from among the Hebrews, so that after the sharpness of Quintilian, the rivers of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto and the smoothness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and practise words that hiss and gasp. What labour I spent on it, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, how often I gave up and then, in my eagerness to learn, began again, my conscience is witness, both mine, who suffered it, and that of those who led their life with me.
passages.notes: The opening "4): c" is the end of a citation (Jerome, Letter [12]4 to Rusticus) plus a quotation mark, and has been left out. The "7" before "verba" is a footnote mark and has been left out. Pliny here is presumably Pliny the Younger.

passages.original: Sanctus Hieronymus ad Principiam scribens tradit, se quoque tum Romam ex Oriente venisse, cum iisdem sanctis episcopis; nam ait de sancta Marcella: a Deniquecum et me Romam, cum sanctis pontifi- cibus Paulino et Epiphanio, ecclesiastica traxisset 8 necessitas (Hier.
passages.english: Saint Jerome, writing to Principia, relates that he too came to Rome from the East at that time, with those same holy bishops. For he says of Saint Marcella: "Finally, when ecclesiastical necessity had brought me too to Rome with the holy bishops Paulinus and Epiphanius" (Jerome,
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-citation; the reference continues in the following text ("Letter 61"). "8" is a footnote mark.

passages.original: audivi Didymum, et in multis ei gratias ago : quod nescivi, didici ; quod sciebam, illo docente non perdidi (Hier. epist. 65). > Atque alibi ad eumdem : « Cum essem Alexandriae, vidi Didymum, et eum frequenter adivi, virum sui temporis eruditissimum ; rogavique eum ut quod Origenes non fecerat ipse compleret, et scriberet in Oseae commentarios; qui tres libros me petente dictavit, quinque quoque alios in Zachariam (Hieron., proæm. in Oseam). » Hactenus ad Parnmachium. Et ad sanctam Paulam : « Dqnique nuper ob hanc vel maxime causam Alexandriam perrexi, ut viderem Didymum, et ab eo in Scripturis omnibus, quae habebam dubia, sciscitarer (Hieron , in proæm.
passages.english: I heard Didymus, and I thank him for many things: what I did not know, I learned; what I knew, I did not lose under his teaching" (Jerome, Letter 65). And elsewhere, to the same man: "When I was at Alexandria, I saw Didymus and visited him often, the most learned man of his time. I asked him to complete what Origen had not done and to write commentaries on Hosea. At my request he dictated three books, and also five others on Zechariah" (Jerome, preface to Hosea). So far to Pammachius. And to Saint Paula: "Finally, I recently went to Alexandria, chiefly for this reason: to see Didymus and to question him about everything in all the Scriptures that I was in doubt about" (Jerome, in the preface to
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-quotation. "Parnmachium" is read as Pammachium and "Dqnique" as Denique. The passage ends mid-citation.

passages.original: » Haec ad Paulam : quibus cum nullam mentionem habeat quod eam comitatus fuerit peregrinantem in Ægyptum, nec alibi, cum de ejusdem Paulae profectione in eamdem provinciam agit, se illi comitem inhaesisse dicat (Ilier. Epist. 27), plane conjectura ducimur, Hieronymum nequaquam cum ea peregrinationem illam suscepisse. Caeterum ad modicum temporis spatium,nempe triginta tantum diebus commoratum esse Hieronymum Alexandriae, Ruffinus exprobrat in invectiva; sed an vere, ipse scit.
passages.english: These are his words to Paula. In them he makes no mention of having accompanied her on her journey to Egypt. Nor does he say elsewhere, when he treats of that same Paula's departure for the same province, that he kept her company as her companion (Jerome, Letter 27). So we are plainly led to conjecture that Jerome by no means undertook that pilgrimage with her. However, Rufinus reproaches [him] in his invective with having stayed at Alexandria only a short space of time, namely only thirty days; but whether truly, he himself knows.
passages.notes: "Ilier." is read as Hier. (Jerome).

passages.original: Vitas Patrum, Pauli, Antonii, Hilarionis et omnium eremitarum, quas tamen vir beatus scripsit Hieronymus, cum omni honore suscipimus.
passages.english: The Lives of the Fathers Paul, Antony, Hilarion and of all the hermits, which the blessed man Jerome wrote, we receive with all honour.
passages.notes: "tamen" is awkward here; it may imply "those, at least, which" Jerome wrote. This sentence resembles the wording of the so-called Gelasian Decree.

passages.original: Cujusmodi sanctus Antonius exstitit, quemadmodum et sanctus Athanasius archiepiscopus meminit in Vita quam de eo conscripsit.
passages.english: What kind of man Saint Antony was, as Saint Athanasius the archbishop also records in the Life that he wrote about him.
passages.notes: The sentence is incomplete as it stands; it reads like a heading or a fragment.

passages.original: « Hujus Ammonis animam postmortem ab angelis in coelum sublatam, Antonius, qui eisdem vixit tempotibus, vidit; quemadmodum ab Athanasio, Alexandriae episcopo, in ejus Vita commemoratum est. »
passages.english: "The soul of this Ammon, after his death, was seen carried up into heaven by angels by Antony, who lived at the same time, as is recorded by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, in his Life."
passages.notes: 'tempotibus' is read as 'temporibus'.

passages.original: Moxque cognovit quod impietatis eorum dogmata, quibus probabantur imbuti,tantam perniciem de eorum cordibus exhalarent. Necmora, viros ipsos insequitur,et apprehensis ait: Unum volo vos interrogare sermonem Qui dixerunt: Interroga. Numquid, ait, Origenis commenta legistis? Qui negantes, : Nequaquam. Quibus ait: Ecce contestor vos coram Domino, quod omnis homo qui legit Origenem, et consentit his quae prave disseruit, in profunda pervenietinferorum, hæreditasque ejus erunt vermes et exteriores tenebrae, quibus iniquoruin animæ sine fine punientur.
passages.english: And at once he learned that it was the doctrines of their impiety, with which they were shown to be imbued, that breathed out so great a corruption from their hearts. Without delay he went after the men themselves, and when he had caught up with them he said: "I want to ask you one thing." They said: "Ask." "Have you," he said, "read the commentaries of Origen?" They denied it: "Not at all." He said to them: "See, I testify to you before the Lord that every man who reads Origen and agrees with what he wrongly taught will come to the depths of hell, and his inheritance will be worms and the outer darkness, in which the souls of the wicked will be punished without end.
passages.notes: 'Qui negantes, :' looks defective; a verb such as 'dixerunt' may have dropped out.

passages.original: Sane notandum est, quia cum quidam legunt in his Actibus quae sanctus Amphilochius scripsit, discrepasse autumant ab his quae sanctus Gregorius Nazianzenus in epitaphio (6) hujus magni viri commemorat, cum alter forte tacuerit quod alter non tacuit, idipsum nobis inter Evangelistas reperientibus. Praesertim cum et idem Amphilochius, qui super tanti viri vita scripserint, haec expositurus apte designet.
passages.english: It should certainly be noted that, when some read in these Acts what Saint Amphilochius wrote, they suppose that it disagrees with what Saint Gregory of Nazianzus records in his funeral oration on this great man, when perhaps one has kept silent about what the other did not keep silent about, which is the very thing we find among the Evangelists. This is especially so since the same Amphilochius, about to set these things out, fittingly indicates those who have written on the life of so great a man.
passages.notes: '(6)' is an editorial footnote mark. The last sentence is obscure; 'scripserint' with 'qui' seems to refer to other writers, and the sense is uncertain.

passages.original: In hujusmodi variissuppliciissacrosancti monachi (13), numero decem et septem, fortes ac tolerantia praeditas animas suas Domino commendarunt. Ex quo perspicue constat animum pietate præditum vitiosis affectionibus imperare, quemadmodum quidam a nostris decretis alienus prodidit(Josephus), se- Bis sacerdotis ac septem filiorum certamina commemorans, qui una cum matre pari omnino sententia praedita pro patriae legis defensione dimicarunt Quibus tolerantiaetanimi magnitudine nihilo inferiores hi eximii Patres ac superae Jerusalem cives exstiterunt.
passages.english: In various tortures of this kind the most holy monks, seventeen in number, commended their brave and enduring souls to the Lord. From this it is plainly established that a mind endowed with piety rules over vicious passions, as a certain man foreign to our teachings (Josephus) has recorded, recounting the contests of an aged priest and seven sons, who together with their mother, all of exactly the same mind, fought in defence of their ancestral law. These outstanding Fathers and citizens of the Jerusalem above proved in no way inferior to them in endurance and greatness of soul.
passages.notes: '(13)' is a footnote mark. 'se- Bis' is read as 'senis' ('aged'). The reference is to 4 Maccabees, traditionally ascribed to Josephus, and to Eleazar and the seven brothers.

passages.original: CAP. XXII.- Valeriano itaque et Gallieno imperantibus, orta seditio de Christianis est, eo quod Cyprianus Carthaginem everteret, et Cornelius Romam. Data est ergo auctoritas ad Paternum proconsulem, ut Cyprianum occideret. Cornelius autem quia a multis Romanis etiam illustribus fovebatur, erat in abditis. Tunc beata Eugenia videns Basillam, ait :' Revelatum est mihi a Domino quod pro virginitate passura sis.
passages.english: CHAPTER 22. So, when Valerian and Gallienus were emperors, an uproar arose concerning the Christians, on the grounds that Cyprian was overturning Carthage and Cornelius Rome. Authority was therefore given to the proconsul Paternus to put Cyprian to death. Cornelius, however, because he was protected by many Romans, including men of rank, was in hiding. Then the blessed Eugenia, seeing Basilla, said: "It has been revealed to me by the Lord that you are to suffer for your virginity."

passages.original: CAP. XV. — Magna vero ferebatur fama per monasteria de domino Pelagio : propterea deliberavi etiam iterato ad eum rrdire, et snlutaribus doctrinis ejus refici. Cumque ad cellulam suam pervenissem, et pulsare, imo nominatim eum interpellare praesnmerem, nihil respondit.
passages.english: CHAPTER XV. — Great was the fame of the lord Pelagius that spread through the monasteries; for this reason I decided to return to him once again and be refreshed by his saving teachings. And when I had reached his little cell and ventured to knock, or rather to call on him by name, he gave no answer.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'rrdire' = redire, 'snlutaribus' = salutaribus, 'praesnmerem' = praesumerem.

passages.original: Nam quod spectat ad profectionem in Ægyptum, cum ipsius Ruffini, necnon Palladii (j) assertione constet Melaniam ac ejus comites, vivente adhuc Athanasio, fuisse Alexandriae, quem liquet hoc ipso anno ex hac vita migrasse, utique ante decimum Valentis annum eam cum suis Ægyptum profectam esse, affirmare necesse est. Quod enim contigerit, ipso vivente adhuc sancto Athanasio, Melaniam Alexandriam pervenisse, Palladius ex eo perspicue demonstrare videtur, cum ait Melaniam ab ipso Athanasio donatam esse ovina pelle, quam dono acceperat a Macario abbate, oblata ipsi munere a leone pro gratiarum actione de catulis caecis ab ipso luci redditis; cujus rei adeo admirandae Ruffinus historiam narrat, qui et ait se praesentem fuisse cum persecutio est illata monachis post Athanasii obitum ab Arianis: « Ea enim, inquit, quae praesens vidi, loquor, et eorum gesta refero, quorum in passionibus socius esse promerui (Ruffin., I.
passages.english: As for the journey to Egypt: since it is established on the statement of Rufinus himself, and also of Palladius, that Melania and her companions were in Alexandria while Athanasius was still living, and it is clear that he departed this life in this very year, it must certainly be affirmed that she set out for Egypt with her companions before the tenth year of Valens. That Melania reached Alexandria while Saint Athanasius was still alive, Palladius seems to show plainly when he says that Melania was given by Athanasius himself a sheepskin, which he had received as a gift from Abbot Macarius; it had been offered to Macarius as a present by a lioness in thanksgiving for her blind cubs, whose sight he had restored. Rufinus tells the story of this remarkable event, and he also says that he was present when persecution was brought upon the monks by the Arians after the death of Athanasius: "For I speak," he says, "of what I saw in person, and I report the deeds of those whose companion in sufferings I was found worthy to be (Rufinus, [Ecclesiastical History] II,
passages.notes: '(j)' is a footnote mark. 'a leone' is literally 'by a lion'; the story of the cubs suggests a lioness. The citation continues in the next passage.

passages.original: At haec de se summa jactantia ab ipso Ruffino esse commenta, exclamat sanctus Hieronymus. cum his recitatis ipsius verbis, sic subdit: Miror quod non adjecerit, rinctus Jesu Christi; et: Liberatus sum de ore leonis ; et: Alexandriæ ad bestias pugnavi ; et: Cursum consummavi, fidem servavi ; super est mihi corona justitiæ. Quæ 427 malum, exsilia, quos iste carceres nominat? Pudet me apertissimi mendacii, quasi carceres et cxsilia absque judicum sententiis irrogentur. Volo tamen ipse scire carceres, et qua- rum provinciarum se dicat exsilia sustinuisse.
passages.english: But Saint Jerome exclaims that these things about himself were invented by Rufinus out of the utmost boastfulness, and after quoting his words he adds: "I wonder that he did not add, 'a prisoner of Jesus Christ'; and 'I was delivered from the mouth of the lion'; and 'I fought with beasts at Alexandria'; and 'I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; there remains for me the crown of righteousness.' What exiles, confound it, what prisons is this man naming? I am ashamed of so obvious a lie, as though prisons and exiles were imposed without sentences from judges. Still, I should like to know the prisons myself, and the provinces in which he says he endured exile."
passages.notes: 'rinctus' is read as 'vinctus'. 'Alexandriae' stands where Paul's text has Ephesus; it is apparently Jerome's deliberate change. '427' is a page number.

passages.original: Laudat sanctus Hieronymus feminae summam constantiam (x), quod simul siccis oculis sepelisset Virum suum ac duos filios (Hieron., epsit. 25) ; uno vero superstite derelicto, peregrinata fuerit in Ægyptum primo, inde Jerosolymam ;
passages.english: Saint Jerome praises the woman's supreme constancy, because she buried her husband and two sons at the same time with dry eyes (Jerome, Letter 25), and, leaving the one surviving son behind, travelled first to Egypt and then to Jerusalem;
passages.notes: '(x)' is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Nec sic quidem ejus hic meminit, quasi tunc Romae esset, quam jam plures ante annos vidimus in Ægyptum primo, inde vero Jerosolymam esse profectam, ibique in praesenti vitam agere : sed idcirco ejus meminit sanctus Hieronymus, quod tum ejus migrationis Jerosolymam occasione, tum Paulae idem iter capessentis, quo et tenebat ipse Hieronymus, detractores eam calumniandi ansam arripuissent. At subdit :
passages.english: Nor does he mention her here as though she were then at Rome, since we have seen that many years before she had set out first for Egypt and then for Jerusalem, and was at present living there. Rather, Saint Jerome mentions her because detractors had seized on a handle for slandering her, both from the occasion of her move to Jerusalem and from that of Paula, who was taking the same journey, the one that Jerome himself was also pursuing. But he adds:

passages.original: Filius ejus unicus illi relictus duxit uxorem Albinam, ex qua Palladius ait genitum esse Melaniam juniorem, senioris Melaniae neptem, quae in matrimonium collocata est Piniano, cujus socrus Albina fuit (Palladius, in Lausiac., cap. 33) ; quod vero ei inhaereret loco matris, sanctus Augustinus ad ipsam scribens, Pinianum ejus filium nominat, et frequenter his uti nominibus consuevit (Aug., epistola 227). Hic rur- sum attende, diversam prorsus hanc Albinam nurum Melaniæ ab illa fuisse Albina matre sanctaMarcellae, de qua sæpe sanctus Hieronymus;
passages.english: Her only son, who was left to her, married Albina, from whom, Palladius says, was born Melania the younger, the granddaughter of the elder Melania, who was given in marriage to Pinianus, whose mother-in-law Albina was (Palladius, in the Lausiac History, chapter 33); but because he clung to her in place of a mother, Saint Augustine, writing to her, calls Pinianus her son, and he was accustomed to use these names frequently (Augustine, letter 227). Here again note that this Albina, the daughter-in-law of Melania, was entirely different from that Albina, the mother of Saint Marcella, of whom Saint Jerome [speaks] often;

passages.original: Accidit autem, dum iidem in Africa morarentur, filium senioris Melaniae vita fungi: quod unicum amissum pignus ita mater modeste flevit, ut magno exemplo fuerit Christianae constandae. De qua summa cum laude rei spectator sanctus Augustinus ad Paulinum Nolanum episcopum scripsit. Non exstat quidem epistola ipsa ; sed ex redditis ad eum ejusdem Paulini litteris, haec omnia, ab aliis silentio obruta, perspicua satis fiunt. Ait enim Paulinus : e Quia docuisti me in spiritu veritatis salvare [servare] moderandi in occiduis mortalibus animi temperamentum ;
passages.english: It happened, moreover, while these same people were staying in Africa, that the son of the elder Melania died: this only pledge [of love], once lost, his mother wept for so modestly that she was a great example of Christian constancy. Of this Saint Augustine, an eyewitness of the matter, wrote with the highest praise to Paulinus, bishop of Nola. The letter itself does not indeed survive; but from the letter of the same Paulinus sent back to him, all these things, which others buried in silence, become clear enough. For Paulinus says: "Because you taught me in the spirit of truth to preserve [keep] a temperate balance of mind in governing [it] amid perishing mortal things;
passages.notes: 'constandae' read as 'constantiae' (constancy). The bracketed [servare] is an editorial alternative reading to 'salvare'; the stray 'e' before the quotation is a scanning artefact for an opening quotation mark.

passages.original: Porro Melariæ huic filio, de quo agimus, uxorem fuisse Albinam nomine, Palladius tradit (Pallad., in Lausiac.), quod et nos superius diximus. Sed in eo omnino Palladium jure correximus ex Paulino et Augustino, dum ait filium hunc senioris Melaniæ valde juvenem secutum matrem fuisse in Siciliam usque, cum regressailla est Jerosolymam ; nam ex his quae dicta sunt satis liquet ipsum matrem secutum in Africam, ibique diem clausisse extremum. Sed et illud (quod majoris momenti est) cujus causa haec notissima ex Paulino de obitu filii Melaniæ recensuisse voluimus;
passages.english: Further, Palladius records that this son of Melania, of whom we are treating, had a wife named Albina (Palladius, in the Lausiac History), which we too said above. But on this point we have rightly corrected Palladius altogether from Paulinus and Augustine, where he says that this son of the elder Melania, as a very young man, followed his mother as far as Sicily when she returned to Jerusalem; for from what has been said it is clear enough that he followed his mother to Africa and ended his last day there. But also that point (which is of greater importance), for the sake of which we wished to review these well-known things from Paulinus about the death of Melania's son;
passages.notes: 'Melariæ' read as 'Melaniae'.

passages.original: Quos inter Adamantius Origenes, Turriano Ruffino interpretatus, sedulo fidei nostrae lectoribus inspiciebatur.Pariter et prout singulis cordi diversa censentes sermocinabantur, cur a quibusdam protomystarum, tanquam scaevus cavendusque tractator improbaretur; quanquam sic esset ad verbum. sententiam translatus, ut nec Apuleius Phaedonem sic Platonis, neque Tullius Ctesiphontem sic Demosthenis in usum regulamque Romani sermonis exscripserint.
passages.english: Among these, Adamantius Origen, translated by Turranius Rufinus, was being diligently examined by readers of our faith. Likewise, as each, holding different views according to their inclination, discussed it, [they asked] why he was disapproved by some of the chief initiates as a perverse author to be guarded against; although he had been translated from word to sense in such a way that neither did Apuleius thus render Plato's Phaedo, nor Tully Demosthenes' [speech on] Ctesiphon, into the usage and rule of Roman speech.
passages.notes: 'protomystarum' (chief initiates/leading clergy) is rare; sense uncertain. 'ad verbum. sententiam' is likely a scanning error, perhaps 'a verbo ad sententiam' or 'ad verbum et sententiam'. 'Ctesiphontem' refers to Demosthenes' On the Crown (in defence of Ctesiphon).

passages.original: et quos fuisse scribit, Origenistas (e) ab episcopis damnatos esse non dubium est; Ammonium videlicet, et Eusebium, et Euthymium (/), et ipsum Evagrium (g), Or (h) quoque et Isidorum (i). et multos alios quos enumerare taedium est. Et juxta illud Lucretii : Ac veluti pueris absinthia terra medentes Cum dare conantur, prius oras pocula circum 447 Contingunt dulci mellis flavoque liquore. Ita ille unum Joannem (j) in ipsius libri posuit prin- cipio, quem et catholicum et sanctum fuisse non dubium est, ut per illius occasionem, caeteros, quos posuerat, haereticos Ecclesiae introduceret.
passages.english: and those whom he writes existed were, without doubt, Origenists condemned by the bishops: namely Ammonius, and Eusebius, and Euthymius, and Evagrius himself, Or also and Isidore, and many others whom it is tedious to list. And according to that [saying] of Lucretius: "And just as physicians, when they try to give children bitter wormwood, first touch the rims around the cups with the sweet golden liquid of honey," so he placed one John at the very beginning of the book, who was without doubt both catholic and holy, so that by occasion of him he might introduce into the Church the others he had included, who were heretics.
passages.notes: Footnote letters (e)–(j) and page number 447 omitted. 'terra' in the Lucretius quotation is a misreading of 'taetra' (foul/bitter).

passages.original: i. Dixit abbas Cassianus : Quia venimus a Palae- stina in Ægypto ad quemdam Patrum (Cassian., I. v Instit., c. 24). Et cum hospitalitatem ncbisinpendisset, interrogavimus eum : Quare tempore susceplionis fratrum regulam jejunii non custoditis, sicut et in Palaestina fit ?
passages.english: 1. Abbot Cassian said: We came from Palestine into Egypt to one of the Fathers (Cassian, Institutes book 5, chapter 24). And when he had shown us hospitality, we asked him: Why, at the time of receiving brothers, do you not keep the rule of fasting, as is done in Palestine?

passages.original: 19. Narravit sanctus Basilius episcopus, dicens : Fuit in quodam monasterio feminarum virgo quaedam, quae stultam esse ac daemonem se habere simulabat (Pallad., c. 41, 42) i Quae usque adeo ab omnibus aliis pro errore habebatur, ita ut nec cibum quidem cum ea caperent.
passages.english: 19. The holy bishop Basil related, saying: There was in a certain monastery of women a certain virgin who pretended to be foolish and to have a demon (Palladius, chapters 41, 42). She was held by all the others to be so deranged that they would not even take food with her.
passages.notes: The ascription to Basil is as the text gives it; 'i' after the citation is a stray mark.

passages.original: Mirati sumus (c) aliquem dubitare num hie Palladius idem sit cum illo quem fuisse natione Galatam et professione Origenistam sanctus Hieronymus tradit; cum idem ipse Palladius eo commentario id profiteatur his verbis (Pallad., cap.22) : « Respondi me esse peregrinum, et de Galatiae partibus venire, et unum ex Evagrii fratribus esse confessus sum.
passages.english: We have been surprised that anyone doubts whether this Palladius is the same as the one whom Saint Jerome reports was a Galatian by nation and an Origenist by profession, since this same Palladius himself professes it in that work in these words (Palladius, chapter 22): "I answered that I was a stranger, and came from the regions of Galatia, and I confessed that I was one of the brothers of Evagrius.

passages.original: ubi aliquandiu moratus haereses docebat Origenis, quem cavendum Epiphanius Joannem ejus loci episcopum quam primum admonuit.Cum vero Origenistarum nullum alium nominet, nisi Palladium, certe, et si alii essent eadem labe conspersi, tamen non alium quam ipsum id muneris subiisse ut Origenis deliramenta doceret, satis apparet. Quamobrem Origenistam illum, quem sanctam Paulam tentasse Hieronymus scribit, neminem certe praeter Palladium tunc in Palaestina morantem fuisse conspicio, de quo ista in ejusdem Paulo epitaphio habet (Hier., epistola 27): « Tangam ergo breviter, quo modo haereticorum coenosos devitaverit lacus, et eos instar habueritethnicorum.
passages.english: where, having stayed for some time, he was teaching the heresies of Origen; Epiphanius warned John, bishop of that place, as soon as possible to beware of him. But since he names no other of the Origenists except Palladius, it is certainly clear enough that, even if others were stained with the same blemish, none other than he undertook the task of teaching the ravings of Origen. Therefore I perceive that that Origenist whom Jerome writes tempted Saint Paula was certainly none other than Palladius, then staying in Palestine, about whom [Jerome] has these words in his epitaph of the same Paula (Jerome, letter 27): "I will touch briefly, then, on how she avoided the muddy pools of the heretics and regarded them as like heathens.

passages.original: V, ad annum Christi 413.— Porro quod iri eam dementiam superbus iste (Pelagius) elatus fuerit, ut assereret esse hominis, vi liberi arbitrii non tantum non peccare, sed etiam non tentari, hinc ipse Hieronymus ex persona Pelagii, ejusque verbis haec ait : a Alii clausi cellulis, et feminas non viden- tes, quia miseri sunt, et verba mea non audiunt, torquentur desideriis ; ego etiam, si mulierum vallor agminibus, nullam habeo concupiscentiam, de me enim dictum est: Lapides sancti volvuntur super terram (Zachar. ix); et ideo non sentio, quia liberi arbitriipotestateChristi trophæum circumfero (Hieron., contra Pelag. I. II) » Hujusmodi plane haereticos visus est idem sanctus Hieronymus alibi suggillasse, dum ait : I Si nota fecissent verba mea populo meo, non blandientes eis, et adulatione perdentes,ut dicerent : Non habetis peccata, perfectam justitiam possidetis, sanctitas et pudicitiaatque justitia in vobis tantummodo reperiuntur; et ego non tradidissem eos in immunditiam et ignominiam, ut facerent quæ non conveniunt, et sequerentur cogitationes suas pessimas.
passages.english: [Baronius, vol.] V, at the year of Christ 413. — Further, that this proud man (Pelagius) was carried away into such madness as to assert that it lies within a man, by the power of free will, not only not to sin but even not to be tempted, is shown from this: Jerome himself, speaking in the person of Pelagius and in his words, says this: "Others, shut up in their cells and not seeing women, are tormented by desires, because they are wretched and do not listen to my words; I, even if I am surrounded by troops of women, have no concupiscence, for of me it was said: 'Holy stones are rolled upon the earth' (Zechariah 9); and so I do not feel [it], because by the power of free will I carry about the trophy of Christ" (Jerome, Against the Pelagians, book II). The same holy Jerome is clearly seen to have taunted heretics of this kind elsewhere, when he says: "If they had made my words known to my people, not flattering them and ruining them with adulation so as to say: 'You have no sins, you possess perfect righteousness, holiness and chastity and righteousness are found in you alone'; then I too would not have handed them over to uncleanness and disgrace, so that they did what is unbecoming and followed their own most wicked thoughts.
passages.notes: The opening 'V' continues 'Baron. t.' in the context (Baronius, Annales, tome V). 'iri' read as 'in'. The stray 'a' and 'I' before quotations are footnote/quotation marks and omitted.

passages.original: Tagastse autem cum esset Pinianus, effusa muni - ficentia adeo ecclesiam illam locupletavit, ut nonnullorum in ejus episcopum Alypium invidiam moverit, prout sanctus Augustinus in epistola ad eum scripta testatur, et ipsa Acta sanctae Melaniae his verbis fidem faciunt: a Civitas autem in qua versabantur appellabatur Tagasta : in qua erat sacrum templum et sacerdos dicendi peritus, et qui oratione multos poterat inducere ad salutem, nomine Alypius;
passages.english: While Pinianus was at Tagaste, he so enriched that church with lavish generosity that he stirred up the envy of some against its bishop Alypius, as Saint Augustine testifies in a letter written to him, and the Acts of Saint Melania themselves confirm in these words: "The city in which they were living was called Tagaste, in which there was a holy church and a priest skilled in speaking, who could lead many to salvation by his discourse, named Alypius;
passages.notes: 'templum' rendered 'church'; 'sacerdos' here means the bishop.

passages.original: Hoc insuper ipso anno, qui sequens est ab Eudoxiaenuptiis,Eudocia mater peregrinata est Jerosolymam voti solvendicausa, ut Socrates tradit his verbis : t Theodosius imperator deinceps (post translationem Joannis Chrysostomi corporis scilicet) preces Christo offerre, quibus gratias pro acceptis beneficiis agat, Christique nomen hoc munere obeundo eximiis honoribus decorare coepit.
passages.english: Moreover, in this very year, which is the one following the marriage of Eudoxia, her mother Eudocia made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem to fulfil a vow, as Socrates relates in these words: "Thereafter (that is, after the translation of the body of John Chrysostom) the emperor Theodosius began to offer prayers to Christ, by which he gave thanks for the benefits received, and by performing this service to adorn the name of Christ with outstanding honours.

passages.original: Hoc autem miraculum narravit beatus Athanasius Alexandriae episcopus, scribens in Vita Antonii, quod cum aliquando monachi ad ipsum missi essent ab Antonio (erat enim in interiore solitudine Antonius), cum ad ipsum venissent, surrexit senex, et ambulabat cum eis. Et cum esset transiturus Lycum fluvium cum ejus discipulo Theodoro, verebatur exui, ne seipsum videret aliquando nudum : et interea dum de ea re dissereret, inventus est trans fluvium, ut qui absque cymba in extasi trajecisset, translatus ab angelo: fratres autem natatu transmiserunt.
passages.english: This miracle was related by the blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, writing in the Life of Antony: that when some monks had once been sent to him by Antony (for Antony was in the inner desert), when they had come to him, the old man rose and walked with them. And when he was about to cross the river Lycus with his disciple Theodore, he was afraid to undress, lest he should at any time see himself naked; and meanwhile, while he was discussing this matter, he was found across the river, as one who had crossed without a boat in ecstasy, carried over by an angel; but the brothers crossed by swimming.
passages.notes: The subject is Amoun (Ammon) of Nitria, not named in the passage. The text says the monks were sent "to him by Antony"; the sense seems to be that Antony sent for him.

passages.original: Hieronymus enim quidam presbyter habitabat in illis locis, qui in sermone Romano magna erat virtute ornatus, et praeclaro ingenio ; sed tanta fuit ejus invidia, ut ab ea obrueretur virtus doctrinae. Cum ergo multis diebus cum eo versatus esset sanctus Posidonius, dicit mihi in aurem :
passages.english: For a certain priest Jerome lived in those parts, who was adorned with great excellence in the Latin tongue and with a brilliant mind; but so great was his envy that the excellence of his learning was overwhelmed by it. So when holy Posidonius had spent many days with him, he said into my ear:

passages.original: Postquam autem hi omnes Roma abscessissent qui catechesi instituti fuerant a beata Melania, barbarica quaedam procella, quae etiam in prophetis jam olim posita fuerat,in Romam irruit,ct nec aeneas quidem statuas reliquit in foro, sed omnia barbarica diripiens insolentia, corrupit; adeo ut Roma quæ mille et ducentis annis pulcherrima fuerat etfrequentissima, dirueretur, fieretque deserta, et ut ait Sibylla, ῥύμη, hoc est vicus, non Roma. Tunc qui catechesi fuerant instituti, et ei minime adversati, Deum laudaverunt qui rerum mutatione persuasisset incredulis,quod aliis omnibus redactis in servitutem, eae solae salvæ fuerint familiæ, quae Domino fuerunt holocausta, studio beatae Melaniae;
passages.english: After all these who had been instructed in the faith by the blessed Melania had left Rome, a barbarian storm, which had long ago been set down in the prophets as well, burst upon Rome, and did not leave even the bronze statues in the forum, but plundering everything with barbarian insolence, ruined [it]; so much so that Rome, which for twelve hundred years had been most beautiful and most populous, was torn down and became deserted, and, as the Sibyl says, a rhymē, that is, a street, not Rome. Then those who had been instructed in the faith, and had not opposed her at all, praised God, who by the change of affairs had convinced the unbelievers that, when all others had been reduced to slavery, those households alone were saved which had become burnt offerings to the Lord through the zeal of the blessed Melania;
passages.notes: Greek ῥύμη (rhymē, "street, lane") is a pun on Rome. "ct" read as "et".

passages.original: Illis annuens,jussit ut hospites ducerent,et ad viam a qua aberrarant reducerent.Nemo autem existimet fabulosam esse narrationem, cum communes veritatis hostes habeatferentes veritati testimonium ; ipsi enim consecuti beneficium, hoc perpetuo cecinerunt; hocque mihi hic magnus narravit Jacobus, dicens se afIuisse, cum hoc beato Maroni narrarent miraculum. Qui ergo non credit Judæis de Cbristianorum miraculis ferentibus testimonium, quomodo non merito vocabitur Judaeisin fidelior? siquidem illi, etiamsi in non sint infesto animo, vincuntur tamen,et cedunt radiis veritatis: hi autem cum existimentur benevoli, et fidei socii neinimicisquidemcreduntvirtutem gratiae testantibus.
passages.english: Assenting to them, he ordered [the lions] to lead the guests and bring them back to the road from which they had strayed. And let no one think the story is a fable, since it has the common enemies of the truth bearing witness to the truth; for they themselves, having received the benefit, have sung of this continually; and this great James related it to me here, saying that he was present when they told this miracle to the blessed Maro. Whoever, then, does not believe Jews bearing witness to the miracles of Christians, how will he not deservedly be called more unbelieving than the Jews? For they, even if they are of hostile mind, are nevertheless overcome and yield to the rays of truth; but these, though they are thought well-disposed and partners in the faith, do not believe even enemies testifying to the power of grace.
passages.notes: "etiamsi in non sint infesto animo" is garbled; the stray "non" contradicts the sense, and it is read as "etiamsi sint infesto animo" ("even if they are of hostile mind").

passages.original: Ad huncipsum abbatemCosmam perrexi ego,dum esset in Laura Pharan; mansi enim in illa annos decem. Cumque mihi loqueretur da salute animae, et quoddam ex dictis sancti Athanasii Alexandriae archiepiscopi allegaret, ait ad me senex : Cum inveneris aliquid ex opusculis sancti Athanasii, nec habue. ris chartas ad scribendum.in vestimentis Luis scribe illud. Tanto talique studio flagrabat erga sanctos Patres nostros, et Joctores sanctus senior.
passages.english: I went to this same abbot Cosmas while he was in the Laura of Pharan; for I stayed in it ten years. And when he was speaking to me about the salvation of the soul, and cited something from the sayings of Saint Athanasius, archbishop of Alexandria, the old man said to me: "When you find something from the little works of Saint Athanasius and have no paper to write on, write it on your clothes." With such great zeal did the holy elder burn toward our holy Fathers and teachers.

passages.original: Idem abbas Irenaeus narravit nobis dicens iterum : Cum venissent barbari in Scythim, recessi inde, et veni in partes Gazae, accepique mihi cellulam in monasterio. Abbas vero ipsa die dedit mihi librum ad legendum, in quo senum gesta (13) scripta erant.
passages.english: The same abbot Irenaeus told us again, saying: "When the barbarians came into Scetis, I withdrew from there and came to the region of Gaza, and took a little cell for myself in a monastery. And that very day the abbot gave me a book to read, in which the deeds of the elders were written.
passages.notes: "Scythim" taken as Scetis in Egypt. "(13)" is an editorial note mark, omitted.

passages.original: Dicebat idem abbas Athanasius : Patres nostri continentiam, et paupertatem, ac nuditatem, rerum omnium usque ad mortem servaverunt; nos autem ventres nostros et crumenas dilatavimus.
passages.english: The same abbot Athanasius used to say: "Our Fathers kept continence, poverty, and stripping themselves of all things until death; but we have enlarged our bellies and our purses."

passages.original: Quod unusquique publice pocuitens ab episcopo suo, de cujus parochia cst, debet suscipere.» Annales Francorum, pag. 29: In absidaecclesiæ. Glossæ veteree : Absida,sedes episcoporum Ibi sedem episcopi fuisso declarat locus Augustini supra, epist.225, ubi praecedit : « an nostra subsellia, rolicta turba, redieram.. »
passages.english: "That each person doing public penance ought to receive [it] from his own bishop, in whose diocese he is." Annals of the Franks, p. 29: "In the apse of the church." Old glosses: "Apse: the seat of bishops." That the bishop's seat was there is shown by the passage of Augustine above, letter 225, where there comes before: "or had I returned to our benches, leaving the crowd..."
passages.notes: The Augustine quotation is fragmentary and its sense uncertain; "an" may mean "or" or introduce a question.

passages.original: » Ex his colligitur Almiridensium civitatem in Scythia esse. Sed apud quem auctorem hujus urbis memoria ? ExistimoAlmiridensium, seu Halmiridensium civitatem dictam a lacu, qui Halmyris Plinio lib. IV, cap. 12, dicitur in hoc tractu : « Ex eodem alveo et super Istropolim lacus gignitur LXIII m. p.ambitu. Halmyrin vocant.» Lacum hunc Danubius facit, quem Pinetus in suo Plinio vulgo vocari ait Lac de Notre Dame de Danubi. id est, lacus divæ Virginis Danubianx. Forte Salmorudis Antonini. Nicephorus, lib. XII, cap.29, post quam dixitEunomium jussu Theodosii Halmyridem deportatum, addit: « Est autem Halmyris Mysiæ in Europa locus, ad Istrum situs.
passages.english: From this it is gathered that the city of the Almiridenses is in Scythia. But in what author is there mention of this city? I think the city of the Almiridenses, or Halmiridenses, was named from the lake which Pliny, book IV, chapter 12, calls Halmyris in this region: "From the same channel, and above Istropolis, a lake is formed, 63 miles in circumference. They call it Halmyris." The Danube makes this lake, which Pinet in his Pliny says is commonly called Lac de Notre Dame de Danubi, that is, the lake of the holy Virgin of the Danube. Perhaps [it is] the Salmorudis of Antoninus. Nicephorus, book XII, chapter 29, after saying that Eunomius was deported to Halmyris by order of Theodosius, adds: "Halmyris is a place of Moesia in Europe, situated on the Ister.
passages.notes: "Antoninus" presumably refers to the Antonine Itinerary.

passages.original: » De Ægyptiorum artaba Fannius : Est etiam terris, quas advena Nilus inundat, Artaba, cui superat modii pars tertia post tres. Namque decem modiis explebitur artaba triplex. Hieronymus, in cap. v Isaiæ : I Pro triginta modiis quos nos pro coro posuimus , qui Hebraice dicimur homer , LXX verterunt ἀρτάας ἓξ, quae mensura Ægyptiaca est, et facit modios viginti. » Plane quadrat æstimatio artabæ apud Hieronymum, cum ea, quae est apud Palladiumjam citatum. Idem, in cap. xi Danielis ; « Ita ut (Ptolemaius Philadelphus) de Ægypto per singulos annos quatuordecim millia et octoginta talenta argenti acceperit, et frumenti ar- tabas (quaa mensura tres modios et tertiam modii partem habet) quinquies et decies cenlena miilia.» Ignotus Græcus libro de ponder et mensuris Αἰγυπτία ϰαὶὁ 'Ιταλιϰὸς ἔχει χοίνϰας η'.«Ægyptia artaba capit modios quinque ;
passages.english: " On the Egyptian artaba, Fannius: "There is also, in the lands which the immigrant Nile floods, the artaba, which exceeds three modii by a third of a modius. For a triple artaba will be filled by ten modii." Jerome, on chapter 5 of Isaiah: "For the thirty modii which we have put for the cor, which in Hebrew is called homer, the Seventy translated six artabas, which is an Egyptian measure and makes twenty modii." Jerome's estimate of the artaba plainly agrees with that in Palladius, already cited. The same [Jerome], on chapter 11 of Daniel: "So that (Ptolemy Philadelphus) received from Egypt each year fourteen thousand and eighty talents of silver, and fifteen hundred thousand artabas of grain (which measure holds three modii and a third part of a modius)." An unknown Greek, in the book on weights and measures: "The Egyptian [artaba] and the Italian [modius] hold eight choinikes." "The Egyptian artaba holds five modii;
passages.notes: The Greek quotation is corrupt and incomplete (likely lacunose); the Latin rendering that follows it ('artaba holds five modii; but the Egyptian and Italian modius holds eight choenices') indicates the fuller sense. "ἀρτάας" read as ἀρτάβας. "dicimur" read as "dicitur".

passages.original: Sed omnino varia mensura fuit artaba. Nam Eupolemus, apud Eusebium, lib. ix, cap. 5 Præpar. Evang., explicans epistolam Ralomonis ait:'0 8i x4po; ἐστὶ ἀρταω̃ν ἔξ : « Corus vero est artabarum sex. » Consule Villalpandum nostrum, Apparatus in Ezechielem parte II, lib.
passages.english: But the artaba was an altogether variable measure. For Eupolemus, in Eusebius, book IX, chapter 5 of the Preparation for the Gospel, explaining the letter of Solomon, says: "The cor is six artabas." Consult our Villalpando, Apparatus on Ezekiel, part II, book
passages.notes: Greek garbled by scanning ('0 8i x4po; = ὁ δὲ κόρος). "Ralomonis" read as Salomonis. Eusebius's Praeparatio book IX chapter number may be inaccurate.

passages.original: Nempe perlapidem specularem tralucebatdecoret ornatus Violae. Et quod clausae essent lecticæ,caveas basternarum vocat Hieronymus epist. 22, ad Eustochium, De custodia virgin.:« Præcedit caveas basternarum ordo semivirorum. » Unde Isaiae LXVI, σϰιάδια vertere LXX,id est,«umbracula,quæ nos dormitoria interpretari possumus vel basternas, » inquit ibi Hieronymus.
passages.english: That is, the beauty and adornment of Viola shone through the transparent stone. And because litters were closed, Jerome, in letter 22 to Eustochium, On the Keeping of Virginity, calls them 'cages of basternae': 'A troop of half-men goes before the cages of the basternae.' Hence in Isaiah 66 the Seventy rendered [the word] as σκιάδια, that is, 'shades, which we can interpret as sleeping-litters or basternae,' as Jerome says there.
passages.notes: 'basterna' was a closed litter carried by mules. 'Violae' is taken as a personal name (Viola); it could also be read as 'of the violet'. The source of the opening sentence is not in the passage.

passages.original: i januarii, habet concursum populi, quis ab exsilio revertenti primus salutaret agnoscendus, quis benedicenti caput supponeret. Palladius, in Vita Chrysostomi : « Ei caput vestrum inclinate,ut Joanni,per omnia. »Ita vidua3diaconissas,utfuturiepiscopi,benedictionem capita inclinato accipiant, monet Chrysostomus.
passages.english: [...] of January, has the crowding of the people, [to see] who would be the first to greet him on his return from exile and be recognised, who would bow his head beneath him as he gave the blessing. Palladius, in the Life of Chrysostom: "Bow your head to him as to John, in all things." Thus Chrysostom admonishes widows and deaconesses to receive the blessing of future bishops with bowed head.
passages.notes: Opening is a fragment ('i januarii'), its beginning lost. 'vidua3diaconissas,utfuturiepiscopi' read as 'viduas, diaconissas, ut futuri episcopi'; the sense of 'futuri episcopi' (genitive, 'of the future bishop'?) is uncertain.

Further, that this kind of garment was made to cover the shoulders and arms is shown by Festus Pompeius under the word Lacerna, when, treating of the lacerna, he says it was smaller than the capitium; and Varro, On the Latin Language, book IV, says the capitium was a women's garment for the chest, so called because it 'takes' (capiat) the chest and encloses the arms; for women who went about without it had their chest and arms bare. That the lacerna was drawn over the tunic, Gellius, book XIII, chapter

passages.original: Item, cap. 136,de sancto Athanasio : accepto suo stichario seu tunica. et birro, Hervetus verterat, accepto suo stichario et cereo. Graece est, λαὼν ἑαυτου̃ τὸ στιχάριον xai τὸ βίῤῥιον. Hervetus ϰηρὸν fortasse legerat.
passages.english: Likewise, chapter 136, on Saint Athanasius: 'taking his sticharion, or tunic, and his birrus [cloak].' Hervetus had translated: 'taking his sticharion and a candle.' The Greek is λαὼν ἑαυτοῦ τὸ στιχάριον καὶ τὸ βίρριον. Hervetus perhaps read κηρόν [wax, candle].
passages.notes: λαὼν is evidently a misprint for λαβὼν ('taking').

passages.original: Ab hoc pane expeditionali seu buccellalo clegan. ter panem, quem benedictionis locotransmittebant, vocarunt Paulinus et Therasiaad Romanianum epistola 36, apud Augustinum : « Ne vacuum fraternae humanitatis officium videretur, de buccellato Christianae expeditionis, in cujus procinctus quotidie ad frugalitatis annonam militamus, panes quinque tibi pariter, et filio nostro Licentio misimus. »
passages.english: From this campaign bread, or buccellatum, Paulinus and Therasia, in letter 36 to Romanianus, found among Augustine's [letters], elegantly named the bread they sent by way of a blessing: 'So that the duty of brotherly kindness might not seem empty, we have sent five loaves to you and likewise to our son Licentius, from the buccellatum of the Christian campaign, in whose array we serve daily for the ration of frugality.'
passages.notes: 'buccellatum' was hard-baked army biscuit.

passages.original: » Item, in Vita sancti Hilarionis, num. 5: » Herbarum ergo succo, et paucis caricis, post triduum vel quatriduum deficientem animam sustentabat. Interpretantur caricas esse ficus siccas.Certe ex Gcuum genere caricas esse docet Plinius, libro XIII,cap. 5: « Syria præter hanc peculiares habet arbores.ln nucum genere pistacia nota.Prodesse adversus serpentium traduntur morsus, et potu et cibo. In ficorum autcm,caricas,et minor ejusgeneris, quae cottana vocant. »
passages.english: Likewise, in the Life of Saint Hilarion, no. 5: 'So with the juice of herbs and a few caricae, after three or four days, he sustained his failing life.' They interpret caricae as dried figs. Certainly Pliny, book 13, chapter 5, shows that caricae are of the fig kind: 'Syria besides this has its own particular trees. Among the nut kind, the pistachio is known. They are said to help against the bites of snakes, both as drink and as food. Among the figs, the caricae, and a smaller one of that kind which they call cottana.'
passages.notes: 'Gcuum' read as 'ficuum'. Opening '»' is a stray mark.

passages.original: Hieronymi habitatio. Vitæ Malchi, num.3 : « Perveni tandem ad eremum Chalcidos, quæ inter Immas et Berrhæam magis adAustrum sita est. » Est in Syria. Hieronymus, epist. 45,ad Chromatium, Jovinum et Eusebium : a Nam postquam, Evagrio transmittente, in ea ad me eremi parte delatae sunt, quæ inter Syros ac Saracenos vastum limitem ducit. » Idem, epist. 51, ad Ruffinum : « Syria mihi velut fidissimus naufrago portus occurrit.
passages.english: Jerome's dwelling. Life of Malchus, no. 3: 'At last I reached the desert of Chalcis, which lies between Immae and Beroea, rather to the south.' It is in Syria. Jerome, letter 45, to Chromatius, Jovinus and Eusebius: 'For after, with Evagrius forwarding them, they were brought to me in that part of the desert which draws a vast boundary between the Syrians and the Saracens.' The same, letter 51, to Rufinus: 'Syria met me like a most trustworthy harbour for a shipwrecked man.'
passages.notes: The subject of 'they were brought' (presumably letters) lies outside the quotation.

passages.original: Apud LXX est: Οἱ δὲ υἱοί 'Ισραὴλ πύξήθησαν, ϰαὶ ἐπληθύνθσαν, ϰαὶ χυδαῑοι ἐγένοντο. Arias Montanus vertit: At filii Israet creverunt et multiplicati sunt, et abundantes fuerunt. Ubi Romana Editio habet : et effusi facti sunt, χυδι̃οι ἐγένοντο., Interpres Origenis : et in multitudine magna diffusi sunt. Χυδαῑον saepe siguificat vulgare, et ex cepio vile. Quare admonet Tbeodoretus,q. i, non esse hoc loco accipiendum quasi per contumeliam dictum, quemadmodum non nulli acceperint; sed tantum numerosam multitudine significare.Ita enim creverunt, inquit, ut per universam illam terram diffunderentur. Aquila ἐξήρποσαν, Symmachus ἐξη̃ρψαν, erepserunt. Eustathius, in Homerum : Χυδαι̌οι, πάλαι ἐλέγονυο οἱ πεπληθυσμένοι, νῡν δὲ ol οὐδσμενοι. « Chydaei olim dicti multiplicati, nunc autem nullius pretii. »
passages.english: In the Seventy it is: Οἱ δὲ υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ ηὐξήθησαν, καὶ ἐπληθύνθησαν, καὶ χυδαῖοι ἐγένοντο. Arias Montanus translates: 'But the sons of Israel grew and were multiplied, and were abundant.' Where the Roman edition has 'and they became poured out', χυδαῖοι ἐγένοντο, the translator of Origen [has]: 'and they were spread abroad in a great multitude.' Χυδαῖον often means common, and by extension worthless. Therefore Theodoret, question 1, warns that in this place it should not be taken as if said in contempt, as some have taken it, but signifies only a numerous multitude. 'For they grew so much', he says, 'that they spread through that whole land.' Aquila [has] ἐξήρπυσαν, Symmachus ἐξῆρψαν, 'they crept out'. Eustathius, on Homer: 'Χυδαῖοι was formerly said of those who were multiplied, but now of those who are worthless.' 'Chydaei were once called the multiplied, but now [those] of no value.'
passages.notes: Several Greek misprints corrected (ηὐξήθησαν, ἐπληθύνθησαν, χυδαῖοι, ἐλέγοντο, οὐδενούμενοι); Aquila's verb form uncertain.

passages.original: Βαστάσας οὗν ἐϰει̃νος ϰεράμια ϰιλιϰίσια. Heraclides,cap.6 : « unius amphorae lagenam bibere coegisset. » Ubi quidam Ms., Cilicencis lagenæ aquam.Apud Athenaenm,lib. III, Cilicii panes, sunt panes magni, quorum etiam meminit Bustatius ad Homerum. Isidorus, lib. xx Orig., cap. 6, meminit Siculævasis. « Lagena et situla Græoanomina sunt, inflexa ex parte ut fierent Latina. Illi enim λάχηνος, nos lagenam ; illi sicila, nos situlam dicimus. » Papias Vocabulista : « Sicula vas aptum ad vinum vel aquam, a Græco tractum,id est sicia.
passages.english: Βαστάσας οὖν ἐκεῖνος κεράμια κιλικίσια ['So he, carrying Cilician earthen jars']. Heraclides, chapter 6: 'he had made him drink a flagon of one amphora.' Where a certain manuscript [has] 'water of a Cilician flagon'. In Athenaeus, book 3, Cilician loaves are large loaves, which Eustathius also mentions on Homer. Isidore, Etymologies book 20, chapter 6, mentions the Sicilian vessel: 'Lagena and situla are Greek names, altered in part so as to become Latin. For they say lagynos, we lagena; they sicula, we situla.' Papias the lexicographer: 'Sicula, a vessel suited for wine or water, drawn from the Greek, that is sicia.'
passages.notes: 'Bustatius' read as Eustathius. The Greek forms quoted from Isidore (λάχηνος, sicila) look garbled; λάγυνος is presumably meant.

passages.original: Hoc cum dixisset, continuo egressus e castris, postera die concitatior reversus est, et Capitolium arsisse clamavit. Arserat autem revera Capitolium. Quod quidem dæmoni et prævidere facile fuit, et celerrime nuntiare. » Sic lib. VIII, cap. 23, docet aude Hermes Trismegistus scire potueritsoperstitiones Ægyptiacas auferendas. Et 1. IX. c. 22, distinguit inter scientiam dæmonum et angelorum, quod angeli « certius temporalia et mutabilia ista noverant, quia eorum principales causas in Verbo Dei conspiciunt, per quod factos est mundos : qui..
passages.english: Having said this, he immediately went out of the camp, and the next day returned more agitated and cried out that the Capitol had burned. And the Capitol had in fact burned. This was easy for a demon both to foresee and to report very swiftly.' So in book 8, chapter 23, he shows from where Hermes Trismegistus could have known that the Egyptian superstitions would be done away with. And in book 9, chapter 22, he distinguishes between the knowledge of demons and of angels: that angels 'know these temporal and changeable things more surely, because they behold their principal causes in the Word of God, through whom the world was made: by which...
passages.notes: 'aude' read as 'unde', 'factos... mundos' as 'factus... mundus'. Passage breaks off mid-quotation.

passages.original: 81, ad Flavianum : « Filius noster Symmachus peracto munere candidati, offert tibi dona quaestoria,et caeteras necessitates nostras pari bonore participat. Quæso igitur ut ejus nominedipthycha et apophoreta suscipere dignemini. a Idem, lib. v, epist. 56, ad Sallustium : » Ad te diptychum candidati, et apophorelicum librarum argenti duarum per hominem tuum misimus, approbare cupientes editioni nostrae te animo non defuisse. Idem, lib. XI, epist. 109 : « Non aspernabere, ut existimo.diptychi et apopboretici oblationem.
passages.english: 81, to Flavianus: 'Our son Symmachus, having completed the office of candidate, offers you quaestorian gifts, and shares our other obligations with equal honour. I ask, therefore, that you deign to accept diptychs and apophoreta in his name.' The same, book 5, letter 56, to Sallustius: 'We have sent you by your man a candidate's diptych and an apophoretum of two pounds of silver, wishing to show that you were not absent in spirit from our show.' The same, book 11, letter 109: 'You will not, I think, spurn the offering of a diptych and an apophoretum.
passages.notes: 'apophoreta': presentation gifts. Text begins mid-reference (book 2, letter 81).

passages.original: Glossarium Camberonense ms. : « Dipticae, dicuaturtabellae, quibus corruptores puellis suis inscribunt amorem. » Papias vocabularista : « Dipticae tabellae, quibus corruptores amorem suum inscribunt puellis. » Apud Ovidium quoque lib. a Amorum, eleg. 15, habes tabellas arcanas ad hanc rcm.
passages.english: The Cambron Glossary, manuscript: 'Dipticae are called tablets on which seducers write their love to their girls.' Papias the lexicographer: 'Dipticae, tablets on which seducers write their love to girls.' In Ovid too, book [2?] of the Amores, elegy 15, you have secret tablets for this purpose.
passages.notes: Book number garbled ('a'); the elegy on tablets is Amores 1.11–12, so the reference is uncertain.

passages.original: Palladius, cap. 84, ait Serapionem Sindonitem Romae »incidisse in quemdam Domnionem.» Forte hic ipse est, cujus memoria in Martyrologio Romano, 28 Decemb. a Romae sancti Domnionis presbyteri, »cujus etiam meminit divus Hieronymus epistola 154, ad Desiderium : « Quod si exemplaria libnerit mutuari, vel a sancta Marcella quae manet in Aventino, vel a Lot temporis nostri Domnione, viro sanctissimo accipere poteris. » Eum etiam ut virum sanctissimum celebrat divus Paulinus, epist. 45, ad Alypium. » Eusebii historiam reperi apud parentem nostrum vere sanctissimum Domnionem.» et post: « Si ipsam membranam sancti Domnionis acceperis, transcriptam nobis remittere dignaberis, » Ad eum..
passages.english: Palladius, chapter 84, says that Serapion the Sindonite "came upon a certain Domnion" at Rome. Perhaps this is the very man whose memory is in the Roman Martyrology on 28 December: "At Rome, [the feast] of Saint Domnion the priest," "whom the divine Jerome also mentions in letter 154, to Desiderius: 'But if you wish to borrow copies, you will be able to receive them either from the holy Marcella, who lives on the Aventine, or from the Lot of our time, Domnion, a most holy man.' The divine Paulinus also celebrates him as a most holy man, in letter 45, to Alypius: 'I found the history of Eusebius with our truly most holy father Domnion.' And afterwards: 'If you receive the parchment itself of the holy Domnion, you will be so good as to send it back to us transcribed.'" To him...
passages.notes: "libnerit" read as "libuerit". The passage breaks off mid-sentence ("Ad eum[dem]"), continued in the following context. The placement of the quotation marks in the edition is confused.

passages.original: GABBARA. Vide de iis dicta Vitam sancti Antonii, o. 57, ubi ea Athanasius describit, et Augustinus nomen prodidit. Vocabulum paucis notum.Pliniusf lib. VII, cap. 16: « Procerissimum hominem ætas nostra divo Claudio principe, Gabbaran nomine. ex Arabia advectum, novem pedum, et todidem unoiarum vidit.
passages.english: GABBARA. See what has been said about these on the Life of Saint Antony, chapter 57, where Athanasius describes them and Augustine gives the name. The word is known to few. Pliny, book VII, chapter 16: "Our age, in the reign of the divine Claudius, saw the tallest man, named Gabbara, brought from Arabia, nine feet and as many inches [tall]."
passages.notes: "o. 57" read as "c. 57"; "todidem unoiarum" as "totidem unciarum".

passages.original: : a Haec autem spiritaliter exponentes, non statim juxta litteram orandi consuetudinem tollimus, qua Deum genu posito auppliciter adoramus, et fixo in terram poplite, magis quod ab eo poscimus impetramus. Legimus enim et Paulum in littore sic orasse, et geniculationcs in oratione præceptas. » Theophilus episcopus Alexandrinus, epistola Paschali 2, contra Origenem : « Genu flectere sollicitæ et humillimae mentis indicium est. »
passages.english: "But in expounding these things spiritually, we do not at once do away with the custom of praying according to the letter, by which we worship God as suppliants on bended knee, and with the knee fixed on the ground obtain all the more what we ask of him. For we read that Paul too prayed thus on the shore, and that kneelings in prayer were commanded." Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, Paschal letter 2, against Origen: "To bend the knee is a sign of an anxious and most humble mind."
passages.notes: The opening quotation is from Jerome on Ephesians 3, as the preceding context shows.

passages.original: Sed et cum tradat auctor in domo Adelphi hospilatum esse Joannem,cum Cucusum in exilium missus esset, plane erroris arguitur; nam licet id ipsum de hospitio Cucusi dicant Leo et Metaphrastes, tamen ipse Chrysostomus (Epistola 13) disertis verbis narrat a Dioscoro se susceptum hospitio, et non ab aliis; licet id complures expetierint.Cum autem haec compingat ea narratione mendacia, quae fides in reliqius?
passages.english: But also, since the author relates that John was lodged in the house of Adelphius when he had been sent into exile to Cucusus, he is plainly convicted of error; for although Leo and Metaphrastes say the same thing about his lodging at Cucusus, nevertheless Chrysostom himself (Letter 13) states in express words that he was received as a guest by Dioscorus, and not by others, although many sought [to do] it. Since, then, he packs such lies into that narrative, what trust [can be placed] in the rest?
passages.notes: 'Adelphi' rendered Adelphius.

passages.original: Vita Pachomii, cap.8 : « Lapsanas enim, id et, agrestia olera, et herbas alias praeter oleum consueverant edere. » Saepe in his libris olera agrestia, quae λαψάναι in Graeco textu, occurrunt. Plinius, lib. xx, cap. 11 : . Inter silvestres brassicas et lapsana est pedalis altitudinis, hirsutis foliis, napi simillimis, nisi candidior esset flore. » Meminit ejusdem Plinius, lib. xix, cap. 8, ubi milites exprobrant imperatori, se lapsana vixisse apud Dyrrhachium.
passages.english: Life of Pachomius, chapter 8: "For they were accustomed to eat lapsanae, that is, wild vegetables, and other herbs, besides oil." Wild vegetables, which are λαψάναι in the Greek text, often occur in these books. Pliny, book XX, chapter 11: "Among the wild cabbages there is also the lapsana, a foot high, with hairy leaves, very like the turnip, except that it would be whiter in flower." Pliny mentions the same in book XIX, chapter 8, where the soldiers reproach their commander that they had lived on lapsana at Dyrrhachium.
passages.notes: "id et" read as "id est". "praeter oleum" (besides oil) is as printed; the sense "without oil" may be intended.

Hence Naarmalcha, that is, 'royal river'. In Ammianus, book

passages.original: Sunt et qui pro itinere unius diei sivediaeta una mansionem ponant, ut cum ait Plinius,lib.xn,c. 14, mansionibus octo distare thuriferam regionem a monte excelso,in quo pagus estSabaeorumAtramitae.
passages.english: There are also those who use 'mansio' [stage] for the journey of one day, or one day's march, as when Pliny says, book XII, chapter 14, that the incense-bearing region is eight stages distant from a high mountain on which there is a village of the Sabaeans, the Atramitae.
passages.notes: "lib. xn" read as "lib. xii".

passages.original: Mafortis meminit etiam Cassianus, lib. vi Instit., cap. 15 : « Praeter colobium, mafortem, caligas, melotem ac psiathium. » lsidorus, lib. xix Origin. A capite 25:« Stola,matronale operimentum, quod cooperto capite et scapula a dextro latere in laevum humerum mittitur.
passages.english: Cassian also mentions the *mafors* [hooded shawl], book VI of the Institutes, chapter 15: "Apart from the *colobium* [sleeveless tunic], the *mafors*, sandals, the *melotes* [sheepskin] and the mat." Isidore, book XIX of the Origins, from chapter 25: "The stola is a matron's covering, which, with the head covered, is thrown from the right side and shoulder onto the left shoulder."
passages.notes: "A capite 25" perhaps a misreading of "cap. 25". The Cassian citation is probably book I, not VI.

passages.original: Omne autem mendacium, etiam officiosum, illicitum esse docet divius Thomas, 2-2, q. 10, art.3, et Augustinus lib. De mendacio, et lib. Contra meadacium, et epist. 86 et 97, apud Hieronymum jam citatis; et in Decreti parte II, causa 22, q. 2, oapite 14, Ne quis arbitretur, allegatur ex Augustino, in psal. v, quod pro temporali vita alicujus nullusmentiri debeat. Quo respicit Alexander II [, in libro v Decretalium Gregorii IX, tit.
passages.english: That every lie, even a helpful one, is unlawful is taught by the divine Thomas, 2-2, q. 10, art. 3, and by Augustine in the book On Lying and the book Against Lying, and in letters 86 and 97 among Jerome's, already cited; and in the second part of the Decretum, cause 22, q. 2, chapter 14, 'Ne quis arbitretur', it is alleged from Augustine, on Psalm 5, that no one ought to lie for the sake of anyone's temporal life. To this Alexander II refers, in book V of the Decretals of Gregory IX, title
passages.notes: Aquinas on lying is 2-2 q. 110, not q. 10; probably a scanning error. The sentence continues in the following context.

passages.original: Puto hæc ita coniliari posse, utdicamusdecimo Ii- bro Stromateon haberi verba illa Origenis quae Hieronymus citat ex lib. vi Stromateon. Sed existimo Hieronymum vocare sextum Stromateon. quia decimam illum Stromateon librum, qui versatur in explanatione Epistolae ad Galatas, adjungitquinque voluminibus quæ proprie scripsit Origenes in Epistolam ad Galatas; atque ita decimus ille adjunctus quinque illis est sextus explanationum in Epistolam ad Galatas. Verba ejus epistolæ 89 sunt: aScripsit Origenes in Epistolam Pauli ad Galatae quinque propria volumina;
passages.english: I think these things can be reconciled thus, by saying that those words of Origen which Jerome cites from book VI of the Stromateis are found in the tenth book of the Stromateis. But I think Jerome calls it the sixth [book] because he adds that tenth book of the Stromateis, which is concerned with explaining the Epistle to the Galatians, to the five volumes which Origen wrote specifically on the Epistle to the Galatians; and so that tenth [book], added to those five, is the sixth of the explanations of the Epistle to the Galatians. His words in letter 89 are: "Origen wrote five volumes of his own on Paul's Epistle to the Galatians;

passages.original: 32: Et caudam cybii, brevesque meenas Cicero, libro II De finibus : « his licet dicere, se a- cipenserem maenae non anteponere. » Plinius, libro X, capite 26: « Mutant colorem candidæ hieme mænae, et Hunt aestate nigriores. » Meminit earum etiam libro XXXII, capite8-12, Persius, Satyra 3 : Maenaque quod prima nondum defecerit orca. Arnobius, lib. III: « Neptunus pistricum dominus atque maenarum. » Oppiano, lib, i dicitur μαινίς.
passages.english: 32: "And the tail of the tunny, and small *maenae* [sprats]." Cicero, book II On Ends: "These may say that they do not prefer the sturgeon to the *maena*." Pliny, book X, chapter 26: "*Maenae*, white in winter, change colour and become darker in summer." He also mentions them in book XXXII, chapters 8–12. Persius, Satire 3: "And because the *maena* in the first jar has not yet run out." Arnobius, book III: "Neptune, lord of sea-monsters and *maenae*." In Oppian, book I, it is called μαινίς.
passages.notes: The "32" continues a Martial citation (book XI, epigram 32?) from the preceding context. Pliny's book reference may be IX rather than X.

passages.original: Cumque hora nona advenisset, secundum consuetudinem complebat omnes orationes suas, et psalmodiam secundum regulam et. ponebat panem ut comederet. a Idem, lib. III, num. 55, in Silvano : « Hora autem nona circumspiciebat frater ille viam, si forte vocaret eum senex ad comedendum. » Idem est apud Pelagium, libello x, num. 69 : Joannes, libello III, n. 2 : « Et circa horam nonam significavit percutiens, et venit ille minor, et fecit modicam cocturam pulmenti. » Augustinus, Regula 2, de tempore edendi : « Operentur autem mane usque ad sextam, et a sexta usque ad nonam reddent Codices;
passages.english: And when the ninth hour had come, he would, according to custom, complete all his prayers and his psalmody according to the rule, and set out bread to eat. The same, book III, no. 55, on Silvanus: "At the ninth hour that brother was looking around at the road, in case the old man might call him to eat." The same is in Pelagius, booklet X, no. 69. John, booklet III, no. 2: "And about the ninth hour he gave the signal by knocking, and the younger one came and made a little cooking of pottage." Augustine, Rule 2, on the time of eating: "Let them work in the morning until the sixth hour, and from the sixth until the ninth let them give back the books;
passages.notes: Stray 'a' omitted. 'reddent Codices' likely means return the books (after reading).

passages.original: 'Εξέλαυνε τη̃ς 'Αντιοχείας μετὰ δυοι̃ν θεράποιν, ὀ μὲν ές τάχος γράϕων, ὀ δὲ ές ϰάλλος. Ejecit ex Antiochia cum duobus servis, quorum alter notarius,alter antiquarius. » Eusebius,Historiae Ecclesiasticæ lib. VI, cap. 2i, de Origene : Ταχογράϕοι γραϕει̃ν ὴσϰημέναις. a Plures quam septem notarii statis temporibus vices suas alternantes dictanti aderant: nec pauciores librarii ac puellae ad eleganter scribendum exercitati.» Idem habes apud Suidam.
passages.english: "He drove out of Antioch with two servants, one writing for speed, the other for beauty." [In Latin:] "He set out from Antioch with two servants, one of whom was a *notarius* [shorthand writer], the other an *antiquarius* [copyist]." Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book VI, chapter 23, on Origen: "Shorthand writers trained in writing. More than seven *notarii* were present while he dictated, relieving one another at fixed times; and no fewer copyists and girls trained to write elegantly." You have the same in the Suda.
passages.notes: The opening Greek quotation (from Philostratus, per context) is followed by a Latin rendering; 'Ejecit' ('he cast out') is evidently meant intransitively, 'he set out'. The chapter number '2i' is presumably 23 (a scanning error); Eusebius' Greek is quoted only in part.

passages.original: A Justiniani ferme tempore (nisi fortasse prius, quod quidem modo non succurrit) dignitati addita est praefectura provinciarum. Qui eo tempore carerent munere provinciae, ac in urbe et senatu praesentes adessent, praesentales patricii,ut est apud Cassiodorum,voca- bantur (Cassiod.. Var, lib. VIII, epist.). Qui praefecturam gerebant, pro suarum quiqueprovinciarummore ac lege nuncupari consueverant, proconsules Africæ, Italiae exarchi, Sicilia strategi, prætores Orientis, etc.
passages.english: From about the time of Justinian (unless perhaps earlier, which does not occur to me at the moment), the prefecture of provinces was added to the dignity. Those who at that time had no provincial office, and were present in the city and the senate, were called *praesentales patricii* [patricians in attendance], as in Cassiodorus (Cassiodorus, Variae, book VIII, letter). Those who held a prefecture were usually named according to the custom and law of their respective provinces: proconsuls of Africa, exarchs of Italy, *strategoi* [generals] of Sicily, praetors of the East, etc.
passages.notes: The letter number in the Cassiodorus reference is missing in the text.

passages.original: Nec singulare aliquid in Macno abstinentiæ exemplum notaretur,si paximadiis vesceretur: plerorumque monachorum in Ægyptois cibu8 fuit. Sed furfnreo pane vesci, hoc inMacno eximium. Rubidum quoque panem apud Plautum, Casina, act. 2,scen. 5. Festus interpretatur parum coctum, quod non quadrat in paximatia, licet Isidorus, lib. xx Orig., cap. 2 recoctum interpretetur. Plautus, in Menaechmis, act. 5, scen. 5, ridicule usurpat panem puniceum et purpureum.
passages.english: Nor would any singular example of abstinence be noted in Macnus if he ate *paximadia* [rusks]: that was the food of most monks in Egypt. But to eat bran bread, that was remarkable in Macnus. Festus interprets the 'reddish bread' in Plautus, Casina, act 2, scene 5, as underbaked, which does not fit *paximatia*, although Isidorus, Origins book XX, chapter 2, interprets it as twice-baked. Plautus, in the Menaechmi, act 5, scene 5, jokingly uses 'crimson and purple bread'.
passages.notes: 'furfnreo' read as furfureo (bran); 'cibu8' as cibus.

Et quidem de neutro hic agitur, sed Pœmenium hic est locus apud Betlheem a pastoribus ita dictus, ubi apparuerunt eis angeli, qui non procul a Bethleem distabat, ut hic apparet, et testatur Hieronymus epistola 27, ad Eustochium : « Haud procul inde Betbleem, descenditad turrem Ader, id est, gregis ; juxta quam Jacob pavit greges suos (Gen. XXXVII), et pastores nocte vigilantes audiremeruerunt: Gloria in excelsis Deo »(Lucæ n), etc. Distat haec turris mille passibus aBethleem, ubi templum erectum est ab Helena, uti testaturNicephorus lib. VIII, cap. 30. Epiphanius Monachus, in Itinerano Jerosolymitano : Ad Orientem Bethleem est conditum monasterium, quod diciturOvile, ubi visus est angelus pastoribns, dixitque ipsis: Cessate a gregibus custodiendis.
passages.english: This solitary of Moschus was one person, the abbot of Palladius another. And indeed neither is in question here; rather, the Poemenium here is a place near Bethlehem, so called from the shepherds, where the angels appeared to them, which was not far from Bethlehem, as appears here, and as Jerome testifies in letter 27, to Eustochium: "Not far from there [is] Bethlehem; she went down to the tower of Ader, that is, of the flock, beside which Jacob pastured his flocks (Gen. 37), and the shepherds keeping watch by night were found worthy to hear: Glory to God in the highest" (Luke 2), etc. This tower is a mile from Bethlehem, where a church was built by Helena, as Nicephorus attests, book VIII, chapter 30. Epiphanius the Monk, in the Itinerary of Jerusalem: "To the east of Bethlehem a monastery has been built which is called the Sheepfold, where the angel was seen by the shepherds and said to them: Cease from guarding your flocks.
passages.notes: 'Poemenium' (from Greek poimēn, shepherd) means 'shepherds' place'. The Jerome quotation seems slightly garbled ('Haud procul inde Bethleem').

II: « Accidit autem ut, juxta quod mos est, ad coqninae officium hebdomadarius deputaretur.» Cassianus, lib.lv Institutionum. c. 19: «Singulis hebdomadibus fratres haec officia sibi reddenda succedunt.» Item: « Has autem septimanas unusquisque suscipiens, usque ad Ccenam Dominici diei ministraturus observat.» De his septimanariis Beu hebdomadariis agit idem Cassianus,libro eodem, capite 20-22,et monet hanc per singulas septimanas culinae inserviendi consuetudinem viguisse in monasteriis Palæstinæ et Mesopotamiae; aliam fuisse consuetudinem in monasteriis Ægypti, ubi certus quispiam toto vitæ suæ tempore culinæ deputabatur, quousque vires suppeterent.
passages.english: Rule: "She who is about to go off her week does the cleaning on Saturday, sweeping away dirt and dust with brooms where necessary." Regino, Chronicle book II: "It happened that, according to custom, he was assigned as weekly server to the duty of the kitchen." Cassian, Institutes book IV, chapter 19: "Each week the brothers succeed one another in these duties to be performed." Also: "Each one, taking on these weeks, serves until the supper of the Lord's day." Cassian deals with these weekly or hebdomadal servers in the same book, chapters 20-22, and notes that this custom of serving in the kitchen week by week flourished in the monasteries of Palestine and Mesopotamia; that there was another custom in the monasteries of Egypt, where one particular person was assigned to the kitchen for his whole life, as long as his strength held out.
passages.notes: 'Hegino' read as Regino (of Prüm). The Rule quoted at the start is that in Hildegard's explanation (from the preceding context).

passages.original: Sibinum quod huc faciat, etiamnum quaero. Noti Σίυνοι genus teli. Justinianus, Novell. 85 : Καὶτοὺς τεϰαλουμένους σιύνους ἤτοι μισιίλια. Et apud Festum : « Sibinam appellant Illyrici telum venabuli simile.» Ennius: I lllyrici restant sicis, sibinisqne fodentes. »
passages.english: What *sibinum* might mean here I am still seeking. The *sibynoi* are a well-known kind of weapon. Justinian, Novel 85: "And the so-called *sibynoi*, that is, missiles." And in Festus: "The Illyrians call *sibina* a weapon resembling a hunting-spear." Ennius: "The Illyrians stand fast, stabbing with daggers and *sibinae*."
passages.notes: The commentator is puzzling over *sibinum* in Moschus' phrase "a tunic of *sibinum*" (see the preceding context). The Greek is garbled by scanning: Σίυνοι and σιύνους stand for σίβυνοι/σιβύνους (the β has dropped out), τεϰαλουμένους for τε καλουμένους, and μισιίλια for μισσίλια (Latin *missilia*, missiles). "I lllyrici" is read as "Illyrici" and "sibinisqne" as "sibinisque". The weapon terms *sibynoi* and *sibina* are left untranslated: they name a spear-like weapon with no exact English equivalent.
